## Claim 1 — Webinar attendance and Pro retention

**Defect: correlation treated as causation (self-selection confound).**
Attendance at a *voluntary* webinar isn't randomly assigned — customers who choose to attend are plausibly more engaged, more invested in the product, or already inclined to stay, for reasons that have nothing to do with the webinar itself. That underlying engagement is a confound that could produce both "attends webinars" and "stays on the plan." Nothing in the memo rules this out (no randomized rollout, no control for account size/tenure/usage, etc.), so "webinars therefore cause higher retention" doesn't follow from an observed association.
*Consequence:* Resources get spent building/running mandatory webinars believing they'll move retention, when the real driver (engagement) goes unaddressed and the program may show no effect at all.

**Defect: the recommendation extrapolates beyond the population that was measured.**
Even if the correlation were causal for the customers who chose to attend, that says nothing about what happens when attendance is *forced* on new customers who wouldn't otherwise opt in. A mandatory requirement changes who attends and why (compliance vs. genuine interest), so the observed 31% gap may not transfer to the new policy at all.
*Consequence:* A mandatory-webinar policy could be rolled out expecting a 31%-type lift and deliver little or nothing, since the mechanism that generated the original number (self-selected, motivated attendees) is removed by making it mandatory.

**Defect: the sample is conditioned on the outcome (survivorship bias).**
The analysis only looks at the 412 customers "still active" today — churned customers are excluded entirely. Measuring a "retention" effect inside a population that has already been filtered down to retained customers is circular and can distort (usually inflate) the apparent size or even the direction of the relationship, since churned webinar-attendees and churned non-attendees are invisible to the comparison.
*Consequence:* The 31% figure may not reflect the true relationship between webinar attendance and churn across the full customer base, leading to a policy justified by a biased estimate.

## Claim 2 — Central region churn (p = 0.04 out of 18 attributes tested)

**Defect: multiple-comparisons / data-dredging problem.**
Eighteen attributes were tested against churn, and one came back significant at p = 0.04. At a conventional 0.05 threshold, testing 18 independent hypotheses gives roughly a 60% chance that at least one will appear "significant" purely by chance (1 − 0.95¹⁸ ≈ 0.60). A single p = 0.04 result out of 18 tests is exactly the kind of finding you'd expect from noise alone, and it would not survive a standard multiple-testing correction (e.g., Bonferroni would require p < ~0.0028). The memo treats this as a confirmed, actionable effect rather than a candidate hypothesis to be validated on new data.
*Consequence:* Quarterly spend gets reallocated to chase a statistical artifact, potentially at the expense of regions/segments where a real effect exists.

**Defect: even if real, correlation with region doesn't establish that spend there reduces churn.**
No mechanism is proposed for *why* Central customers churn less, and no causal link is drawn between "more spend" and "even lower churn." Region could be a proxy for something else (industry mix, account size, contract type) that's the actual driver.
*Consequence:* Spend is directed at a geography rather than the underlying factor, likely producing no incremental benefit even if the original correlation is genuine.

## Claim 3 — Satisfaction rose 62% → 66%

**Defect: causal attribution to "the new support model" without ruling out alternative explanations.**
A single quarter-over-quarter change is asserted to be caused by one specific initiative, with no comparison group, no historical baseline for normal quarter-to-quarter fluctuation, and no accounting for other things that changed that quarter (seasonality, pricing changes, product releases, survey response bias, sample composition). No significance test or confidence interval is given, so there's no basis for concluding this movement is anything other than ordinary noise.
*Consequence:* Continued investment/credit is given to a support initiative that may have had no real effect, while the actual cause of the improvement (or its absence) goes unidentified — and if the "improvement" is just noise, it may reverse next quarter, undermining confidence in whatever program gets credited.

## Not flagged
I did not raise the "62%→66% = 4% improvement" phrasing as a defect since you noted the numbers themselves are correct and it's plausibly meant as a percentage-point difference rather than a computational error — but it's worth being explicit in the memo that this is a 4-point (≈6.5% relative) change, since "4% improvement" can be read either way when it's later relied on to justify next quarter's decisions.
